title: Sleep: why we need it, and how a bedtime routine helps

summary.text: Learn eight picture pairs at bedtime, go to sleep, and in the morning most of them are still in your head. While you sleep, your brain keeps what you learned, your body grows, and it mends small hurts. Your child tests their memory across a night and across a day, and finds out that humans and nearly every other animal sleep, even a jellyfish with no brain. Then they make a bedtime routine that helps them fall asleep.
summary.art: A girl of seven asleep in a dark bedroom, with eight small picture cards on the table beside her bed, and a window showing the night sky.

intro.hook: Think about last night. You lay down and closed your eyes. The next thing you knew, it was morning. What was your body doing all that time?
intro.text: Most children say 'nothing'. But a sleeping body is busy. In this unit we test what happens to things you learn when you sleep on them. We find out which animals sleep, and how. We also learn why we need sleep at all, and how a bedtime routine helps you fall asleep.
intro.art: A boy of seven sitting up in bed in the morning, rubbing his eyes, with a clock on the wall and sunlight on the floor.

outcomes: By the end I can say three things sleep does: it helps my body grow, it helps my body mend and fight germs, and it helps me keep what I learned.
By the end I can say that a child of my age needs about 9 to 12 hours of sleep every night.
By the end I can do the picture-pairs test, compare a night of sleep with a day awake, and say what I found.
By the end I can name signs that someone is sleepy, and signs that they slept too little.
By the end I can name humans and other animals that sleep, and say how some of them sleep.
By the end I can make a bedtime routine and say why each step helps.

terms.meaning: Sleep is a long rest every day. You lie still, your eyes close, and you notice much less of what is around you. A loud noise or a shake can wake you.
terms.example: You sleep at night. A baby also sleeps many times in the day.
terms.art: A child asleep on a mat with a light sheet, and a fan turning slowly above.

terms.meaning: Memory is how you keep what you learned or saw, so you can bring it back later.
terms.example: You remember your friend's name, the way to the shop, and the words of a song.
terms.art: A girl humming a song, with small pictures of a friend, a shop and music notes in a bubble above her head.

terms.meaning: Growth hormone is a body chemical that helps children grow. Your body makes most of it in deep sleep, soon after you fall asleep.
terms.example: Children grow taller year by year, and much of that growing is helped along at night.
terms.art: A sleeping child with a faint ladder of height marks on the wall beside the bed.

terms.meaning: A routine is the same steps done in the same order, again and again.
terms.example: Brushing your teeth, then putting on night clothes, then a story, every night, is a bedtime routine.
terms.art: Three small pictures in a row: a toothbrush, night clothes and a story book, joined by arrows.

terms.meaning: Your body clock is the way your body keeps time through a day and a night. It helps you feel sleepy at night and awake in the morning.
terms.example: If you go to bed at the same time every night, you start to feel sleepy near that time.
terms.art: A child yawning at night beside a round clock drawn inside the outline of a body.

terms.meaning: A nap is a short sleep in the day.
terms.example: Grown-ups may nap after lunch. Small children nap in the afternoon.
terms.art: A person napping on a chair after lunch, with glasses resting on their lap.

terms.meaning: A yawn is a big, slow opening of the mouth with a deep breath in. People yawn more when they are sleepy or bored.
terms.example: At bedtime you may yawn again and again.
terms.art: A girl in night clothes stretching her arms and yawning widely.

explanations.definition: Sleep is a long, regular rest in which the body lies still and notices much less of the world, and from which it can be woken.
explanations.description: When you sleep, your eyes close and your muscles go soft. You do not hear quiet sounds, like the fan or a car outside. A loud sound or a shake wakes you up quickly. That is how sleep is different from fainting, when a person cannot be woken easily. Every night you sleep for many hours, and then you wake by yourself. Your brain stays busy all night.
examples: A child in deep sleep may not hear the pressure cooker whistle in the next room, but wakes when shaken and called by name.
A cat curled up asleep pricks up their ears when a bowl is put down.
A grown-up asleep on a night bus wakes when the conductor calls their stop.
explanations.context: This card says what sleep is, and how you can tell someone is asleep.
explanations.art: A child asleep in bed with soft muscles and closed eyes, and small sound lines from a fan that stop before reaching her ear.

explanations.definition: Sleep helps the body grow and mend, helps it fight germs, and helps the brain keep what was learned that day.
explanations.description: Soon after you fall asleep, you go into deep sleep. In deep sleep your body makes most of its growth hormone, which helps you grow. Sleep also helps your body mend small hurts and fight germs. People who sleep too little catch colds more easily. And sleep helps memory. Scientists find that children who sleep after learning something remember more of it than children who learn it in the morning and stay awake all day. The picture-pairs test lets you check this for yourself.
examples: After a night of good sleep, a new song you practised at bedtime often comes out easily in the morning.
A child who slept badly is often cranky, slow and forgetful the next day.
When you are ill with fever, you feel like sleeping much more than usual.
explanations.context: This card says three things sleep does for your body and your brain.
explanations.art: A sleeping child with three small pictures around the bed: a growing height chart, a plaster on a knee, and a thought bubble holding picture cards.

explanations.description: Nearly every animal that scientists have studied sleeps, or rests in a way like sleep. A sleeping animal is easier to catch, so sleep must matter a lot. But scientists still argue about its main job. Here are three ideas. Each one may be part of the answer.
examples: Crows fly to big trees at dusk and sleep there together.
A fruit fly kept awake at night rests more the next day.
An upside-down jellyfish, who has no brain, pulses more slowly at night.

perspectives.who: Chiara Cirelli and Giulio Tononi, sleep scientists in the USA
perspectives.explanation: During the day, the brain makes many new links between its cells as you learn. Sleep trims back the weak links and keeps the strong ones, so the brain is ready to learn again.

perspectives.who: Maiken Nedergaard, Lulu Xie and their team, in 2013
perspectives.explanation: In sleeping mice, fluid washed waste out of the brain much faster than in mice that were awake. So sleep may be a time for the brain to clean itself. In 2024, another team found the opposite in mice, so this idea is now argued about.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study animals in the wild
perspectives.explanation: Sleep keeps an animal still and safe at the time of day when they cannot find food well, and it saves energy.

explanations.context: This card is about a question nobody has fully answered: why humans and other animals need sleep at all.
explanations.art: Three small panels: a brain with links being trimmed, a brain with water washing through, and a bat asleep in a dark cave.

explanations.concept: How a bedtime routine helps you fall asleep
explanations.definition: A bedtime routine is the same few calm steps, in the same order, at about the same time every night.
explanations.description: If you go to bed at the same time every night, you start to feel sleepy near that time. Calm steps, like a wash, brushing teeth and a story, tell your body that sleep is coming. Dim light helps too. Bright light, from a tube light or a phone held close, tells your body it is still day. In 2009, Jodi Mindell and her team asked families of babies and small children to keep a short bedtime routine. Within two weeks, the children fell asleep faster and woke less in the night.
examples: A bath, night clothes, brushing teeth, one story and lights off, at 8:30 every night.
Turning off the TV in the hall half an hour before bedtime.
Opening the curtains in the morning to let in daylight, so the body clock knows the day has begun.
explanations.context: This card says how doing the same calm steps every night helps you fall asleep.
explanations.art: A strip of four pictures: a child washing her face, brushing teeth, listening to a story under a dim lamp, and asleep with the light off.

explanations.concept: How humans and other animals sleep
explanations.definition: Humans and other animals sleep in many different ways, places and times.
explanations.description: Humans are animals, and like most other animals we sleep every day. But each kind of animal sleeps in their own way. Bats sleep in the day, hanging upside down by their feet. House crows fly to the same big trees every evening and sleep there in a crowd. Many birds turn their head round and tuck their beak into their back feathers. Most fish have no eyelids, so they rest with their eyes open. At night, a honeybee rests very still, and her antennae droop. Even some plants, like the touch-me-not and the tamarind, fold their leaves at night. Charles Darwin called this 'sleep movements'.
examples: A newborn baby sleeps for about 14 to 17 hours in a day, in short bits.
A child of 7 needs about 9 to 12 hours of sleep every night.
Most grown-ups need at least 7 hours.
explanations.context: This card is about the many ways humans and other animals sleep.
explanations.art: A night picture: a bat hanging upside down, crows crowded in a big tree, a parrot with her beak tucked in, and a child asleep at a window.

agreed.text: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night.
agreed.evidence: In 2016, a group of children's sleep doctors in the USA looked at hundreds of studies. Children who slept this much paid attention and learned better, managed their moods better, and had fewer injuries.

agreed.text: Sleep helps us keep what we learned.
agreed.evidence: In many studies, people learn pairs of words or pictures, then either sleep or stay awake for the same number of hours. Those who slept remember more. This has been found in children aged 6 to 8 too.

agreed.text: Nearly every animal that has been studied sleeps, or has a rest like sleep.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have found sleep in mammals, birds, fish, fruit flies, bees and tiny worms. In 2017, they found a sleep-like state in a jellyfish.

agreed.text: Too little sleep makes it harder for the body to fight germs.
agreed.evidence: In a study in 2015, grown-ups who slept less than 6 hours a night were more likely to catch a cold when given the cold germ than those who slept 7 hours or more.

challenging.claim: When you sleep, your brain switches off.
challenging.for: When you sleep you do not notice the room, and in the morning the night seems blank.
challenging.against: Scientists who record the brain's signals find the brain busy all night. In some parts of sleep it is nearly as busy as when you are awake. That is also when the most vivid dreams happen.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea about the sleeping brain.

challenging.claim: Watching a phone or TV in bed helps you relax and fall asleep.
challenging.for: A favourite show can feel calming, and some people say it helps them stop worrying.
challenging.against: Most studies find that children who use screens in bed go to sleep later and sleep less. Scientists still argue about how much is because of the bright light, and how much is because the show is exciting.
challenging.context: This card is about screens at bedtime.

challenging.claim: You can make up for lost sleep by sleeping very late at the weekend.
challenging.for: After a short night, a long sleep does make you feel better.
challenging.against: A long lie-in moves your body clock later, so Sunday night's sleep comes late. Studies find that a lie-in helps a little, but does not undo a whole week of short nights.
challenging.context: This card is about catching up on sleep.

big_questions.q: In the morning, the picture pairs were still in your head. Who was keeping them while you slept?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether you need to be aware of something for your mind to work on it.

big_questions.q: An upside-down jellyfish has no brain, but rests like sleep every night. If sleep is not only for brains, what else might it be for?
big_questions.hint: Think about the jellyfish's whole body, which senses light, food and touch.

big_questions.q: When you are in deep sleep and not dreaming, where are you?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you remember of the night, and what was still going on in your body.

big_questions.q: Why do you think nearly every animal sleeps, even though a sleeping animal is easier to catch?
big_questions.hint: Think about how crows sleep together in one big tree, and bats in a dark cave.

big_questions.q: Does everyone in your home need the same amount of sleep?
big_questions.hint: Think about a baby, a child, a parent and a grandparent.

story.title: Nila and the Blinking Green Light
story.note: Nila, Sachin, Amma and Chithi Kavitha are made up. The facts in the story are true: children of seven need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep, sleep helps people keep what they learned, and a sleep-like state was found in upside-down jellyfish in 2017.
text: Nila was seven. She lived in a flat on the fourth floor in Chennai, with Amma and her little brother Sachin. Sachin was five.
That week, Nila was learning a new song for the school Pongal function. The song had four lines. She knew the first three. But every time she reached the last line, the words went muddled.

On Monday night, Nila lay in bed and could not sleep. The TV was on in the hall. A green light blinked on the wifi box near her bed. Blink. Blink. Blink. She took Amma's old phone and watched cartoons under the sheet until very late.

On Tuesday morning, Nila was cross. She spilled her milk. She forgot her water bottle. At school, she could not remember even the first line of the song. In the afternoon, she fell asleep at her desk.
That evening, Chithi Kavitha came to stay. Chithi was Amma's younger sister. She was a nurse at a big hospital, and some weeks she worked at night.
'You look tired, Nila,' said Chithi.
'I am not tired,' said Nila, and yawned a huge yawn.
Chithi laughed. 'Your yawn says something different. How long did you sleep last night?'
Nila counted on her fingers. 'From very late until seven. Maybe seven hours.'

'A girl of seven needs about nine to twelve hours,' said Chithi. 'Sleep is not a waste of time. While you sleep, your body grows. It mends small cuts and fights germs. And your brain does something else. It keeps safe what you learned in the day.'
'Even the song?' asked Nila.
'Even the song. Let's try something. Tonight we will do a bedtime routine. A routine is the same calm steps, in the same order, every night.'
Together they made a list. Wash, night clothes, brush teeth, sing the song once, a story, lights off. Nila drew a little picture for each step and stuck the list on her door.

At half past eight, Amma turned off the TV in the hall. Nila washed and brushed her teeth. She sang the song, and the last line was still muddled. Chithi stuck a small piece of paper tape over the blinking green light. 'There,' she said. 'Now your room is dark.'
'Tell me a story,' said Nila.

So Chithi told her a true one. 'Some years ago, three students in America looked at jellyfish in a tank at night. These jellyfish rest upside down on the sand and pulse to move water. A jellyfish has no brain at all. Many people thought only animals with a brain could sleep. But at night the jellyfish pulsed more slowly. They were slow to notice when they were moved. And when the students kept them awake all night, the jellyfish were sleepy the next day.'
'Jellyfish sleep?' said Nila, and her eyes were already closing.
'Jellyfish sleep,' said Chithi softly. 'Crows sleep. Bats sleep. Sachin sleeps. Goodnight.'
In the morning, Nila woke up by herself before Amma called. Sun came in through the window. She sat up and began to hum. Then she sang the whole song, all four lines, without stopping.
She stopped and stared. 'Chithi! I sang the last line right! I did not even practise it this morning.'
Chithi smiled. 'You practised it at bedtime. Then you slept. While you slept, your brain went over it and kept it.'
'But I did not know my brain was doing that,' said Nila.
'No,' said Chithi. 'You were asleep. A lot of your mind's work happens when you are not watching.'
Nila thought about that. Then she ran to tell Sachin. 'Sachin! Your brain works at night, even when you are snoring!'
'I do not snore,' said Sachin, and yawned.
story.epiphany: Nila could not sing the last line at bedtime, but after a full night's sleep she sang it right without practising. She sees that her brain kept and sorted what she learned while she slept, even though she knew nothing about it.
ask: Why was Nila cross and forgetful on Tuesday?
Which steps were in Nila's bedtime routine? Why did Chithi cover the green light?
How did Nila know that sleep had helped her with the song?
art: A girl under a sheet at night, lit by a phone screen, with a green light blinking on a wifi box beside her bed.
A woman in a nurse's uniform and a girl sticking a list of bedtime pictures onto a bedroom door.
A girl sitting up in bed in morning sunlight, singing with her arms wide, while her aunt smiles from the door.

games.title: Who Sleeps How? A matching pairs game
games.context: This is a memory game about how humans and other animals sleep. Half the cards name an animal. The other half say how someone sleeps. Turn over two cards at a time and find the pairs.

img.credit: Devika M B, CC BY, via iNaturalist
Suhel Quader, CC BY, via iNaturalist
Utain Pummarin, CC BY, via iNaturalist

printables.title: 8 sleep cards to cut out
items: I sleep in the day, hanging upside down by my feet.
At dusk I fly to a big tree and sleep in a crowd.
I curl up for many naps in the day, and my ears prick up at a sound.
At night I keep very still and my antennae droop.
I have no brain, but at night I pulse slowly and rest.
I turn my head round and tuck my beak into my back feathers.
I am a human baby. I sleep about 14 to 17 hours a day, in short bits.
Like most fish, I have no eyelids, so I rest with my eyes open.

rules: Cut out all 16 cards. Mix them and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
Take turns. Turn over two cards and read them aloud. A grown-up can read for a child who cannot read them yet.
If one card is an animal and the other says how that animal sleeps, keep the pair and have another go.
If they do not match, turn them face down again in the same places. Try to remember where they are.
When all the pairs are found, the player with the most pairs wins. If you tie, you both win.
Play again tomorrow morning. Do you remember more places after a night's sleep?

setup.art: Sixteen small cards face down in four rows of four on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 16 cards face down in 4 rows.

setup.art: A girl holding up two cards, one with the word Bat and one saying 'hanging upside down by my feet'.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Is it a pair?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Read each card aloud once with your child. 3. Mix them and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
flow.say: These cards show how humans and other animals sleep. Let's read them all once. Then we hide them and look for pairs.
flow.kid: Read every card once. Then turn them all face down.

flow.do: Take turns to turn over two cards. Keep a pair. Turn non-pairs back over in the same place.
flow.say: Turn over two. Is this the bat and the bat's sleep card? If not, try to remember where they are.
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Do they match? Remember where they were.
flow.parent: This game uses memory, just like the picture-pairs test. Say aloud where each card was when you turn it back. That helps everyone remember.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Ask which way of sleeping surprised your child most.
flow.say: Which animal sleeps in the most surprising way? Why do you think they sleep like that?
flow.kid: Which animal surprised you? Why do they sleep that way?

ask.q: Why might crows sleep together in one tree?
good: So many eyes can spot danger.
It is safer in a crowd.
They can find each other in the morning.

games.title: Sleepy or Wide Awake? A bedtime sorting game
games.context: This is a sorting game about bedtime. Some cards show things that help you fall asleep. Others show things that keep you awake. Sort them, then build a bedtime routine from the helpful ones.

items.b: Helps. A wash is calm, and the body cools down after it, which helps sleep.
Helps. It is a calm step that tells your body bedtime is near.
Helps. Soft, loose clothes are comfortable to sleep in.

items.f: Reading a story with a dim lamp
items.b: Helps. Dim light and a calm story get you ready to sleep.
Helps. A dark room tells your body it is night.

items.f: Going to bed at the same time every night
items.b: Helps. Your body clock learns the time and makes you sleepy then.
Helps. Quiet, slow sounds calm the body.
Helps. Talking about worries can calm you down.
Keeps you awake. Bright light and exciting shows push sleep later.
Keeps you awake. Running makes your heart beat fast. Play hard earlier in the day.

items.f: A big plate of sweets at bedtime
items.b: Keeps you awake. A big meal just before bed can make sleep hard, and sugar on teeth at night is bad for them.

items.f: Bright tube light on in the bedroom
items.b: Keeps you awake. Bright light tells your body it is still day.

items.f: Loud TV in the next room
items.b: Keeps you awake. Noise can stop you falling asleep and wake you up.
Keeps you awake. Your body clock cannot learn when to make you sleepy.

printables.title: Two sheets to draw on paper
items: A dark blue sheet with a moon: 'Helps me sleep'
A bright yellow sheet with a lightning bolt: 'Keeps me awake'

rules: Lay the two sheets on the floor. Mix the cards and stack them face down.
Take turns. Turn over the top card and read the front aloud. A grown-up can read for a child who cannot read it yet.
Guess which sheet the card goes on, and say why.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. Put the card on the right sheet, even if you guessed wrong.
When all 14 cards are sorted, take the 8 'Helps me sleep' cards. Choose five and put them in the order you would do them at bedtime.
That is your own bedtime routine.

setup.art: A dark blue sheet with a moon and a yellow sheet with a lightning bolt on the floor, with a stack of cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two sheets. Stack the cards.

setup.art: Five cards laid in a row on the blue sheet: wash, teeth, night clothes, story, lights off.
setup.caption: 2. Put five helpful cards in order. That is a routine.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and draw the two sheets. Mix the cards.
flow.say: Some things help us fall asleep. Some things keep us awake. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Some things help you sleep. Some keep you awake. Let's sort them.

flow.do: Take turns to turn a card, guess where it goes and say why. Then read the back aloud and put the card on the right sheet.
flow.say: Where does this card go? Why do you think so? Now let's read the back.
flow.kid: Where does this card go? Say why. Then read the back.
flow.parent: Watching a phone in bed is the card children argue about most. Many feel it relaxes them. Let them say so, then read the back. Studies find that children with screens in bed sleep later and less.

flow.do: Your child picks five 'Helps me sleep' cards and lays them in order as a routine.
flow.say: Now make your own routine. Which five steps would you do, and in what order?
flow.kid: Pick five helpful cards. Put them in your bedtime order.

experiments.title: Sleep on It: does a night's sleep help you keep picture pairs?
experiments.context: In this experiment your child learns two sets of eight picture pairs. They learn the day set in the morning and are tested at bedtime, after a day awake. They learn the night set at bedtime and are tested the next morning, after a night of sleep. Then you compare how many pairs they kept.
experiments.question: Will you keep more picture pairs after a night of sleep, or after a day awake?
experiments.predict: You will learn one set in the morning and one set at bedtime. Which set will you remember better the next time you are tested? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both sets have eight pairs of simple things. We learn both sets the same way, going through them twice. We test each set straight after learning, and again about 11 hours later. Only one thing changes: whether those hours are spent awake or asleep. Two things are not quite fair. At bedtime you may be tired when tested. And one set may be a little easier than the other. So we also look at how many you knew straight after learning, and if you repeat the test, you swap the sets.

materials.item: 16 pieces of paper, each about the size of your palm
two envelopes or two folded sheets of newspaper, to keep the sets apart
a clock or a phone, to note the times

schedule.what: Morning: draw the cards, then learn the day set and test it straight away.
Bedtime: test the day set. Then learn the night set, test it straight away, and go to sleep.
Morning: test the night set. Compare the two sets.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Your child draws two rows of eight boxes, one for each set, and colours a box for every pair they remembered later.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Day set: learned in the morning

setup.art: A child and a parent drawing simple pictures on folded paper cards: an elephant on the left half and an umbrella on the right, a mango and a bus.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two sets of eight picture pairs, one pair on each folded card.

setup.art: A parent holding up two cards side by side while a girl names them aloud at a table in the morning.
setup.caption: 2. Morning: learn the day set. Test it at bedtime.

setup.art: A girl in night clothes on her bed naming picture cards her parent holds up, with a dim lamp on.
setup.caption: 3. Bedtime: learn the night set. Then sleep.

setup.art: The same girl in the morning, naming the partner of a cat card, with a score sheet beside her.
setup.caption: 4. Next morning: test the night set. Compare.

flow.do: 1. Fold 16 pieces of paper in half. 2. On each one, draw a quick picture on the left half and a different picture on the right half. The two lists are in the parent note. 3. Share the drawing: your child draws as many as they like, and you draw the rest. 4. Keep the two sets of eight cards in separate envelopes.
flow.say: We are making two sets of picture pairs. The pictures in a pair do not belong together. That makes them a real test of memory.
flow.kid: Draw one picture on each half of a card. The two pictures are a pair.
flow.parent: Day set: elephant and umbrella, mango and bus, star and shoe, fish and chair, kite and spoon, tree and cup, auto and flower, drum and banana. Night set: cat and clock, boat and key, moon and bucket, parrot and ball, coconut and bell, house and leaf, lamp and frog, egg and ladder. Quick, simple drawings are fine. A pair of things that do not go together, like a mango and a bus, is harder to guess. So the test shows real memory, not good guessing.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before you start.
flow.say: You will learn the day set now and the night set at bedtime. Which set will you remember better later? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which set will you remember better? Why?

good: The day set, because I am fresh in the morning.
The night set, because I will sleep on it.
Both the same, because it is the same number of hours.

flow.parent: Write the guess in the table. Many children guess the day set, because they feel sharper in the morning. That is a good reason. Let the test answer it.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, open each day-set card and show it for a slow count of 5. 2. Your child says both names aloud. 3. Go through all 8 cards twice. 4. Then fold each card so only the left picture shows, mix the cards, and ask for the partner of each. 5. Write down how many are right.
flow.say: Look at the pair. Say both names. Elephant and umbrella. Now I show you only the elephant. What was with it?
flow.kid: Look at each pair. Say both names. Then say the missing partner.
flow.parent: Do not correct wrong answers in the test, and do not practise the cards during the day. Note the time. Put the envelope away.

flow.wait: Do this at bedtime, about 11 hours after the morning test.
flow.do: 1. At bedtime, before lights off, test the day set the same way. 2. Fold each card, mix them, and show only the left picture. 3. Write down how many are right. 4. Do not show the pairs first.
flow.say: Do you remember the day set from this morning? I show the first picture. What was its partner?
flow.kid: Here is the first picture. What was its partner?
flow.parent: Test in the same way as the morning: show the first picture and wait for the partner's name.

flow.do: 1. Now learn the night set the same way: each card for a count of 5, twice. 2. Test straight away and write down how many are right. 3. Put the envelope away and go to sleep.
flow.say: Now the night set. Look, and say both names. Then we will test them, and you go to sleep.
flow.kid: Learn the night set now. Then go to sleep.
flow.parent: Do this as the last thing before lights off. No screen afterwards. Note the time.

flow.wait: Do this the next morning, about 11 hours later.
flow.do: 1. In the morning, test the night set. 2. Write down how many are right. 3. Fill in the 'pairs lost' column for both sets.
flow.say: You slept on the night set. Let's see how many you kept. What was with the cat?
flow.kid: What was with the cat? Say each partner.
flow.parent: Most children lose a pair or two over a day awake, and lose fewer or none over a night of sleep. If both sets came out the same, that is a real result too. One child and one try is a small test. Do it again with new pairs on another day, and this time learn the night set in the morning and the day set at bedtime. Then add up both tries.

flow.do: Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why. Then tell them what scientists found.
flow.say: Which set did you keep better? What tells you? Scientists find that sleep helps the brain keep what you learned that day.
flow.kid: Which set did you keep better? Sleep helps your brain keep what you learned.

check.q: In many studies, which set do children usually remember better?
options: The set learned in the morning, after a day awake
The set learned at bedtime, after a night of sleep
check.why: In many studies, children and grown-ups keep more of what they learned when they sleep soon after learning. During the day, new things crowd in and some pairs are lost.

flow.parent: A strong answer has a claim, evidence and a reason. For example: 'Sleep helped me keep the pairs. I lost 2 day pairs but no night pairs. My brain kept them while I slept.'

experiments.title: The Yawn Test: does seeing a yawn make you yawn?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up yawns again and again while your child watches. Another time, the grown-up smiles instead. Your child counts their own yawns each time.
experiments.question: Will you yawn more while you watch someone yawn, or while you watch someone smile?
experiments.predict: Will you yawn more while watching yawns, or while watching smiles? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each watch lasts 3 minutes. The grown-up does it at the same distance, in the same room and the same light. Only one thing changes: yawning or smiling. We do the smiling watch first, so the yawns do not carry on into it.
results_table: How many times I yawned in 3 minutes

materials.item: a clock or a phone timer
paper and a pencil for tally marks

schedule.what: Watch 3 minutes of smiles, then 3 minutes of yawns, and count.

experiments.record: Draw a tally mark for each yawn. Draw two faces, one smiling and one yawning, and write your count under each.

setup.art: A parent smiling at a girl sitting opposite her on the floor, with a phone timer between them.
setup.caption: 1. Watch a grown-up smile for 3 minutes. Count your yawns.

setup.art: The same parent yawning widely while the girl watches and makes a tally mark.
setup.caption: 2. Watch a grown-up yawn for 3 minutes. Count again.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: I am going to smile at you for 3 minutes, then yawn for 3 minutes. When will you yawn more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: When will you yawn more? Why?

good: Yawns spread from one person to another.
Smiles make me smile, so yawns make me yawn.
No difference, I yawn when I am tired.

flow.do: 1. Sit facing your child. 2. Look at them with a gentle smile for 3 minutes, without yawning or talking. 3. Your child makes a tally mark each time they yawn.
flow.say: Watch my face. Each time you yawn, make a mark.
flow.kid: Watch the face. Make a mark when you yawn.

flow.do: 1. Now yawn, a big slow yawn every 15 seconds or so, for 3 minutes. 2. Your child keeps counting.
flow.say: Now watch me again, and keep counting your yawns.
flow.kid: Watch again. Count your yawns.

flow.do: Compare the two counts. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: When did you yawn more? What does that tell you about yawns?
flow.kid: When did you yawn more? What does that tell you?
flow.parent: Many people, and many children of 6 and older, yawn after seeing a yawn. This is called contagious yawning. Some people do not, and that is a real result too. Nobody knows for sure why yawns spread. One idea is that it helps a group get sleepy, or wake up, at the same time. Your child may be a little more tired in the second watch. To check, do the test again another day with the yawns first.

check.q: When do people usually yawn more?
check.why: Seeing someone yawn often makes people yawn too. Even reading about yawns can do it. Nobody knows for sure why.

activities.title: My Bedtime Routine Strip: five steps, seven nights
activities.context: In this activity your child draws their own bedtime routine as a strip of five pictures. They stick it on the bedroom door and tick each step every night for a week.

materials.item: a long strip of paper, or two sheets taped end to end

schedule.what: Draw the five steps, stick the strip on the door, and follow it tonight.
Follow the strip and tick each step.
Follow the strip and tick each step.
Follow the strip and tick each step.
Follow the strip and tick each step.
Follow the strip and tick each step.
Follow the strip, tick the last night, and talk about how bedtimes went.

activities.record: The strip with ticks for seven nights, and one sentence about how falling asleep changed. Your child says it and you write it.

setup.art: A long paper strip with five boxes: a bucket of water, a toothbrush, night clothes, a book under a dim lamp, and a moon.
setup.caption: 1. Draw five bedtime steps in order.

setup.art: The strip taped on a bedroom door, with ticks in pencil under each box.
setup.caption: 2. Stick it on the door. Tick each step every night.

flow.do: Talk about what your child does at bedtime now. Choose five calm steps together, ending with lights off.
flow.say: What do you do before you sleep? Let's choose five calm steps, and do them in the same order every night.
flow.kid: Choose five calm steps for bedtime. The last one is lights off.

flow.do: Your child draws one step in each box, then you stick the strip on the bedroom door.
flow.say: Draw one step in each box. Then we will stick it where you can see it.
flow.kid: Draw one step in each box. Stick it on your door.
flow.parent: Agree on a bedtime too, such as 8:30. Children of 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. Count back from the time they must wake.

flow.wait: Do this every night for seven nights in all, starting tonight.
flow.do: Follow the strip each night. Your child ticks each step as it is done.
flow.say: Which step comes next? Tick it when it is done.
flow.kid: Do each step. Tick it.

flow.do: On the seventh night, look at the ticks together.
flow.say: Was it easier to fall asleep this week? Which step helped most?
flow.kid: Was it easier to fall asleep? Which step helped most?

good: Lights off, because the dark made me sleepy.
The story, because it calmed me down.
Going to bed at the same time.

activities.title: The Dark Room Hunt: find every light at bedtime
activities.context: In this activity your child turns off the lights at bedtime and lies in bed. They count every light they can still see, then find a way to cover or block each one.

materials.item: paper tape or a small piece of paper and tape

activities.record: A list of every light found, and what you did about it. The count before and after.

setup.art: A dark bedroom seen from the bed, with a glowing dot on a charger, a blinking light on a wifi box and a streetlight glow at the curtain edge.
setup.caption: 1. Lie in bed in the dark. Count every light you see.

setup.art: A child sticking a small piece of paper tape over a glowing light on a charger while a parent holds a torch.
setup.caption: 2. Cover or block each light. Count again.

flow.do: 1. At bedtime, turn off the lights. 2. Your child lies in bed for one minute while their eyes get used to the dark. 3. They count every light they can see, and you write them down.
flow.say: Lie still for one minute. Then look round the room. How many lights can you still see?
flow.kid: Lie still in the dark. Count every light you can see.

flow.do: 1. With a torch, go to each light. 2. Decide together how to block it. 3. Tape over a small glow, close the curtain, or shut the door to the hall.
flow.say: This light is on the wifi box. How could we stop it shining on your bed?
flow.kid: Find each light. How can you block it?
flow.parent: Never cover anything that gets hot, like a lamp or a plug that warms up. Small indicator lights on chargers, fans and wifi boxes are safe to cover with paper tape.

flow.do: Turn the lights off again. Count the lights your child can still see.
flow.say: Now how many lights can you see? Why does a dark room help you sleep?
flow.kid: Count again. Why does the dark help you sleep?

ask.q: Why does a dark room help you sleep?
good: Dark tells my body it is night.
Light can keep me awake.
Nothing blinks at me.

activities.title: Crows Going to Bed: a window watch at dusk
activities.context: In this activity your child watches the sky from a window or balcony just before sunset. In many Indian cities, crows fly in lines to a few big trees to sleep together. Your child counts the crows that fly past in five minutes. Do this if you can see some sky from home.

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of the sky
paper and a pencil for tally marks

activities.record: A tally of crows in five minutes, an arrow showing which way they flew, and the time.

setup.art: A girl at a flat window at sunset making tally marks, with a line of crows flying across an orange sky.
setup.caption: 1. At dusk, watch the sky for 5 minutes.

setup.art: A big tree at dusk crowded with dark crows on every branch.
setup.caption: 2. Crows fly to big trees to sleep together.

flow.do: 1. About 20 minutes before sunset, stand at a window. 2. For 5 minutes, your child makes a mark for every crow flying past. 3. Note which way most of them fly.
flow.say: Watch for crows. Make a mark for each one. Which way are they going?
flow.kid: Watch the sky. Mark each crow. Which way are they flying?
flow.parent: House crows in many Indian cities gather in big groups in a few tall trees to sleep, called a roost. If you see none, try another evening, or look for other birds settling into trees or ledges. Look at the sky away from the Sun, never straight at it.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: Where do you think the crows are going? Why might they sleep all together?
flow.kid: Where are the crows going? Why sleep together?

good: To be safe from owls and cats.
Many eyes can watch for danger.
To stay warm or find friends.

projects.title: Ask the Family: who sleeps how long?
projects.context: In this project your child asks people in the family how long they slept last night, and their age. Then they draw a picture chart to see whether younger people sleep longer.

materials.item: a notebook page with a table
a phone, to call a relative or friend who lives far away
crayons and paper for the chart

schedule.what: Make the table. Ask two or three people at home.
Ask two or three more people, in person or on a call.
Draw a moon for each hour slept, and compare.

projects.record: A table of names, ages and hours slept, and a chart with a row of moons for each person.

setup.art: A girl with a notebook asking an older relative a question at the breakfast table.
setup.caption: 1. Ask each person their age and how long they slept.

setup.art: A chart with a row of small moons next to each family member's name, a long row for a baby cousin and shorter rows for adults.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one moon for every hour of sleep.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with three columns: name, age, hours slept last night. 2. Fill in the first row for your child. 3. Then your child asks you, and one or two more people at home. If few people live with you, ask a neighbour.
flow.say: Ask each person two questions. How old are you? What time did you sleep and wake up?
flow.kid: Ask: how old are you? How long did you sleep?
flow.parent: Help your child count the hours from bedtime to waking. If someone napped in the day, add a note.

flow.do: Your child asks two or three more people, at home or on a phone call.
flow.say: Who else can we ask? A neighbour, a cousin, an aunt or a grandparent, in person or on a call?
flow.kid: Ask more people. Write their answers.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws one moon for every hour each person slept. 2. Line the rows up from youngest to oldest. 3. Talk about the pattern.
flow.say: Who has the longest row of moons? Who has the shortest? What do you notice about their ages?
flow.kid: Draw a moon for each hour. Who slept longest?

good: Babies and children sleep longer.
Grown-ups sleep less.
An older person slept less at night but napped after lunch.

flow.parent: Most families find that younger children sleep longest. Older people often sleep less at night and nap in the day. A child of 7 needs about 9 to 12 hours. If nobody in your list is a baby, the pattern may be weak. That is still a result.

challenges.title: A Sleep Kit for the Overnight Train
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. Your family is taking an overnight train from Chennai to Kochi. The coach lights stay on for a while, people talk, and the train rattles. Can you pack a sleep kit from home things, and plan a bedtime routine that works on a train?
challenges.problem: Plan a bag of home things and a short routine that will help you fall asleep on a busy night train.
constraints: Use only things you already have at home.
The kit must fit in one small cloth bag.
Keep at least three steps of your home bedtime routine.
materials: home things to test, like a dupatta, a soft cap and a small book
general: An eye cover made from a folded dupatta or a soft cloth, to block the light.
Night clothes or a soft T-shirt to change into.
A toothbrush, so the brushing step stays the same as at home.
creative: A favourite small pillow or soft toy from your own bed, so the smell and feel are like home.
A storybook from home, read at the same time as your usual bedtime.
A soft cap or scarf pulled over the ears to make the noise quieter.
challenges.your_turn: Now pack your own sleep kit. Draw what is in the bag, and tell a grown-up the three routine steps you will keep. The grown-up writes them down. Try it at home tonight with the lights on and the radio playing.

setup.art: A child packing a small cloth bag with a folded dupatta, a toothbrush, a soft toy and a storybook.
setup.caption: 1. Pack your sleep kit.

setup.art: A child asleep on an upper berth of a train with a dupatta over her eyes and a soft toy beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Use it on the train, at your usual bedtime.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. List what makes sleep hard on a train.
flow.say: What could stop you sleeping on a night train?
flow.kid: What makes it hard to sleep on a train?

good: The lights stay on.
People talk and the train rattles.
The bed is not my own.

flow.do: Your child chooses things for the kit and draws them. They also pick three routine steps to keep.
flow.say: What will block the light? What will make the noise quieter? Which steps from home will you keep?
flow.kid: Pick things to block light and noise. Pick three home steps.
flow.parent: Do not put cotton or anything small inside the ears. A soft cap or scarf over the ears is safer. Tie the eye cover loosely, and never round the neck.

flow.do: Test the kit at home: lie down with the lights on and a radio playing softly.
flow.say: Does the eye cover make it feel dark? Does the cap make the noise quieter?
flow.kid: Try your kit. Does it feel darker and quieter?

videos.title: Why do we need sleep?
videos.why: Shows in simple words that sleep helps the body grow and mend and the brain keep what was learned.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why Do We Need Sleep? | SciShow Kids" by SciShow Kids, 3 minutes, 33 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Do jellyfish sleep?
videos.why: Shows real Cassiopea jellyfish pulsing on the sand, and how the Caltech team tested their sleep-like state in 2017.
videos.check: Found by search: "Do Jellyfish Sleep?" by caltech, 2 minutes, 19 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Thousands of crows flock to roost at dusk
videos.why: Shows a large crow roost filling up at dusk in Burnaby, Canada, for children who cannot see one from home.
videos.check: Found by search: "Thousands of crows flock to Burnaby every day to roost. Witness their spectacular journey." by CBC British Columbia, 4 minutes, 7 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: How many hours of sleep does a child of 7 need each night?
quiz.why: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours. Newborn babies sleep more, and grown-ups need at least 7.

quiz.p: Your body makes most of its growth hormone at one time. When?
opts: In deep sleep, soon after falling asleep
quiz.why: Most growth hormone is made in deep sleep, early in the night. That is one reason children need long, good sleep.

quiz.p: Meena, a girl in Class 2, learned a new song at bedtime and slept well. What is most likely in the morning?
opts: She has forgotten all of it
She remembers it well, maybe better than at bedtime
She can only sing it backwards
quiz.why: Sleep helps the brain keep what you learned that day. Many people find a new song or step comes out easier after a night's sleep.

quiz.p: In the picture-pairs test, why did we test each set straight after learning it too?
opts: To see how many pairs you knew at the start, so we can count how many were lost
quiz.why: Counting at the start and later tells us how many pairs were lost. Then the two sets can be compared fairly, even if one was learned better.

quiz.p: Which of these is a sign that someone is sleepy?
quiz.why: Yawning, rubbing eyes, feeling cross and finding it hard to pay attention are signs of being sleepy.

quiz.p: Arjun went to bed very late. What will he most likely be like the next day?
quiz.why: Too little sleep makes people cranky, slow to react and forgetful. It also makes it easier to catch a cold.

quiz.p: At night, a honeybee rests very still. What happens to her antennae?
quiz.why: Honeybees that are resting or asleep keep still and their antennae droop. Scientists first noticed this in the 1980s.

quiz.p: An upside-down jellyfish has no brain. What did scientists find in 2017?
opts: The jellyfish has a sleep-like rest every night
The jellyfish sleeps only in winter
quiz.why: At night the jellyfish pulsed more slowly and were slower to respond. Kept awake all night, they were sleepy the next day. So sleep does not need a brain.

quiz.p: Which bedtime step helps your body clock most?
opts: Going to bed at the same time every night
Having a different bedtime every night
Watching a bright screen in bed
quiz.why: Your body clock learns your bedtime, and makes you sleepy near it. A different time every night confuses it.

quiz.p: Kavya's room has a bright tube light on until she falls asleep. What would help her most?
opts: Switching to a dim lamp, then lights off
quiz.why: Bright light tells the body it is still day. Dim light, then dark, tells the body night has come.

quiz.p: What does your body clock do?
opts: It makes you sleepy at night and awake in the morning
It tells you the time on the wall
quiz.why: Your body clock keeps time through a day and a night. It helps you feel sleepy at night and awake in the morning.

worksheets.title: What sleep does, and the picture-pairs test

items.p: Draw a line from each job to what sleep does.
pairs: Your body makes growth hormone in deep sleep
Small cuts and bruises heal, and the body fights germs
Your brain keeps what you learned in the day
items.why: These are three things scientists agree sleep does for children.

items.p: Draw your two rows of eight boxes from the picture-pairs test. Colour a box for each pair you remembered later.
items.a: Two rows, with the night-set row usually having as many or more coloured boxes.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both sets side by side, so the difference is easy to see. If both rows are the same, that is a real result too.
items.art: Two empty rows of eight small boxes, one labelled 'Day set' and one labelled 'Night set'.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: which set did you keep better, and what does that tell you about sleep?
items.a: For example: 'The night set. I lost 2 day pairs and 0 night pairs. Sleep helped me keep them.'
items.why: A strong answer names the set, gives the numbers as evidence, and links the result to sleep helping memory.

items.p: When you are asleep, your brain stops working until morning.
items.why: False. The brain is busy all night. It keeps memories and does other work, and in some parts of sleep it is nearly as busy as when you are awake.

items.p: If you sleep very late on Sunday morning, it fully makes up for a whole week of short nights.
items.why: False. A long lie-in helps a little. But it moves your body clock later, and it does not undo a whole week of short nights.

items.p: In the picture-pairs test, the mango was paired with a bus. Why did we pair things that do not go together?
opts: So you could not just guess the partner
items.why: If the pairs went together, like a cup and a saucer, you could guess. Odd pairs test real memory.

items.p: Here is a child's bedroom at night. Write 'block' next to each light that could keep the child awake. Say your labels, and a grown-up writes them.
items.a: 'Block' next to the wifi box light, the phone screen, the streetlight at the curtain edge and the open door to the bright hall.
items.why: Any light near the bed can tell the body it is still day. Covering small lights and closing curtains and doors makes the room dark.
items.art: A bedroom at night with a glowing wifi box, a phone lit up on the bed, light coming in at the curtain edge, and a bright hall through an open door.

items.p: In the picture-pairs test, both sets had 8 pairs and both were learned twice. Why?
opts: So the only thing that changes is awake or asleep
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it is whether the hours after learning are spent awake or asleep.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl of 7 in Madurai, and her cousin Ravi, who is 8, are talking about bedtime.

views.says: I watch cartoons in bed. It makes me feel calm, so I sleep better.
Screens in bed keep you awake. A story with a dim lamp is better.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right. A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: 'Lakshmi, because studies find children with screens in bed sleep later and less.' Then it is fair to Ravi: a show can feel calming, and scientists still argue about how much the light itself matters.
items.why: Both have a point. Most studies agree with Lakshmi, but Ravi is right that feeling calm matters for sleep.

items.p: In the story, Nila slept for about 7 hours. A girl of 7 needs at least 9 hours. How many hours short was she?
items.why: Count on from 7 to 9: 8, 9. That is 2 more hours. 9 take away 7 is 2.

worksheets.title: Sleep in humans and other animals, and a routine that works

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to how they sleep.
pairs: In a crowd in a big tree
items.why: Each animal sleeps in their own way. Most fish have no eyelids, so their eyes stay open as they rest.

items.p: Upside-down jellyfish have no brain. Scientists say they still have a sleep-like rest. What did the scientists see that made them say so? A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: At night they pulsed more slowly. They were slower to respond when moved. After a night kept awake, they were sleepy the next day.
items.why: A strong answer gives at least two of the three tests. Each test shows one sign of sleep.

items.p: Some plants fold their leaves at night. Draw a tamarind or touch-me-not branch in the day, and the same branch at night.
items.a: The day branch has leaves spread open. The night branch has the leaves folded together.
items.why: Darwin called this 'sleep movements'. A strong drawing shows the same branch twice, open and then folded.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, one labelled 'Day' and one labelled 'Night'.

items.p: Farhan, a boy of 8, sleeps at 9 on school nights and at midnight on Saturday. Why might Sunday night be hard?
opts: His body clock moved later, so he is not sleepy at 9 on Sunday
He has too much sleep stored up
items.why: A very late night moves the body clock later. On Sunday night, his body is not ready to sleep at the usual time.

items.p: Humans are animals, and nearly every other animal that scientists have studied also sleeps.
items.why: True. Scientists have found sleep, or a rest like sleep, in mammals, birds, fish, fruit flies, bees, worms and jellyfish.

items.p: Your friend says, 'Sleep is a waste of time. I could play more if I did not sleep.' What would you tell her? A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: For example: 'Sleep is not wasted. My body grows and mends while I sleep, and my brain keeps what I learned. Without sleep I would be cross and forget things.'
items.why: A strong answer gives at least two jobs sleep does, and maybe evidence from the picture-pairs test.

items.p: Sort these by who usually needs the most sleep: a newborn baby, a child of 7, a grown-up.
items.why: Babies need about 14 to 17 hours a day, children of 6 to 12 about 9 to 12 hours, and most grown-ups at least 7.

items.p: Priya, a girl in Class 2, did the yawn test. She yawned 4 times while watching yawns and once while watching smiles. What does this show?
opts: Seeing a yawn made her yawn more
items.why: She yawned more while watching yawns. Many people yawn after seeing a yawn. This is called contagious yawning.

items.p: Revathi, a nurse in Chennai, works at night and sleeps in the day. Her daughter Anu, who is 7, sleeps at night.

views.says: People should sleep at night, when it is dark. Sleeping in the day is wrong.
My body can learn to sleep in the day, if I make my room dark and keep the same times.
I sleep at night with my flock, and a bat sleeps all day. Every animal has a time.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Why? Then say what another view gets right. A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view with a reason, for example: 'Revathi, because the body clock can learn a new time, and bats sleep in the day.' Then it is fair to Anu: night is the easiest time for most humans, and night workers often find it harder to sleep well.
items.why: Most humans sleep best at night, but bodies can shift, and other animals sleep at other times. Each view has part of the truth.

items.p: Here is a night train berth. Label two things in the sleep kit and what each one blocks. Say your labels, and a grown-up writes them.
items.a: For example: 'dupatta over the eyes blocks light' and 'soft cap over the ears makes noise quieter'.
items.why: A strong label names the thing and the trouble it fixes: light, noise or a strange bed.
items.art: A child lying on a train berth with a cloth over her eyes, a soft cap over her ears and a soft toy beside her, with arrows pointing to each.

applications: Doctors who care for children ask about sleep, because poor sleep can look like trouble with paying attention.
Hospitals plan nurses' and doctors' night shifts so that workers get time to sleep in between.
Bus and lorry drivers are told to stop and rest, because a sleepy driver reacts slowly.
Many schools think about start times, because children who sleep enough learn better.

open_questions.q: What is the main reason humans and other animals sleep?
open_questions.why_open: Sleep helps memory, growth, mending and saving energy. Scientists still argue about which job came first, and whether there is one main job.

open_questions.q: Does sleep clean waste out of the brain?
open_questions.why_open: A study in mice in 2013 found that it does. A study in mice in 2024 found the opposite. Scientists are still testing it.

open_questions.q: Why do yawns spread from one person to another?
open_questions.why_open: Many people yawn after seeing a yawn, and some do not. Nobody knows for sure why, or why yawning happens at all.

ask_kids: What did you remember this morning that you learned yesterday?
Which animal near our home is asleep right now?
How did you feel today after last night's sleep?
What is your favourite step in your bedtime routine?
Why do you think babies sleep so much?

jokes.j: Why did the bat sleep upside down?
jokes.a: So their dreams would not fall out!

jokes.j: What did the pillow say to the tired child?
jokes.a: Rest your head, I've got you covered!

jokes.j: Why did the crow go to the big tree at night?
jokes.a: Their whole flock was having a sleepover!

jokes.j: Why did the jellyfish go to bed early?
jokes.a: They did not need a brain to know they were tired!

jokes.j: What do you call a dinosaur who is fast asleep?
Why did the clock go to bed?
jokes.a: It was wound up all day!

jokes.j: Why did the picture cards stay up late?
Why was the yawn so popular?

maths.problem: In the picture-pairs test, Divya knew 7 day pairs straight after learning and 5 at bedtime. She knew 7 night pairs at bedtime and 7 the next morning. How many pairs did she lose from each set?
maths.answer: She lost 2 day pairs and 0 night pairs.
maths.explain: 7 take away 5 is 2, so 2 day pairs were lost. 7 take away 7 is 0, so no night pairs were lost. She kept the night set better.
maths.context: This is about the picture-pairs test, where you learned one set in the morning and one at bedtime.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how many pairs were lost, so we can compare the two sets fairly.

maths.problem: Meena, a girl of 7, goes to bed at 8 in the evening and wakes at 7 in the morning. A child of her age needs 9 to 12 hours. Is she getting enough?
maths.answer: Yes. She sleeps 11 hours, which is between 9 and 12.
maths.explain: From 8 to 12 midnight is 4 hours. From 12 to 7 is 7 hours. 4 and 7 make 11.
maths.context: This is about counting the hours from bedtime to waking.
maths.why_maths: Counting hours on a clock tells us whether a bedtime gives enough sleep.

maths.problem: In a family sleep survey, a baby slept 15 hours, a girl of 7 slept 10, her mother slept 7 and her grandmother slept 6. Put them in order from most sleep to least. What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: Baby 15, girl of 7 10, mother 7, grandmother 6. The younger the person, the more they slept.
maths.explain: 15 is the biggest number, then 10, then 7, then 6. The ages go the other way, from youngest to oldest.
maths.context: This is about the project where you asked your family how long they slept.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order helps us see a pattern between age and sleep.

maths.problem: Four children did the yawn test. While watching smiles, they yawned 0, 0, 1 and 0 times. While watching yawns, the same children yawned 3, 0, 4 and 1 times. How many of the four yawned more while watching yawns?
maths.answer: Three of the four. The second child yawned 0 times both ways.
maths.explain: Compare each child: 3 is more than 0, 0 is the same as 0, 4 is more than 1, and 1 is more than 0. So three children yawned more. Yawns spread to many people, but not to everyone.
maths.context: This is about the yawn test, where you counted yawns while watching a grown-up yawn or smile.
maths.why_maths: Comparing counts for each child shows whether a pattern holds for most people, or only for some.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that an animal without a brain can sleep? This card tells the true story of three students and a tank of jellyfish.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many scientists thought sleep was something brains do. Sleep had been found in mammals, birds, fish, fruit flies and tiny worms, and all of them have a brain or a knot of nerve cells that works like one. Upside-down jellyfish, called Cassiopea, have no brain at all. They have only a loose net of nerve cells across their body. They rest upside down on the sand and pulse their bell to move water. In 2016, three students at Caltech, a university in the USA, wondered whether these jellyfish sleep. They were Claire Bedbrook, Ravi Nath and Michael Abrams. They filmed the jellyfish day and night. At night, the jellyfish pulsed about a third less. When the students gently moved a resting jellyfish at night, the jellyfish was slower to respond than in the day. And when the students squirted water at them through the night to keep them awake, the jellyfish were less active the next day, like a tired child. Their teachers, Viviana Gradinaru, Lea Goentoro and Paul Sternberg, helped them publish the work in 2017. It showed that sleep does not need a brain.
how_we_found_out.who: Claire Bedbrook, Ravi Nath and Michael Abrams, students at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), with Viviana Gradinaru, Lea Goentoro and Paul Sternberg
how_we_found_out.when: 2016 (the tests) and 2017 (published in the journal Current Biology)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Sleep needs a brain, so only animals with a brain or a knot of nerve cells can sleep.
how_we_found_out.art: A glass tank with several upside-down jellyfish resting on sand, pulsing their bells, while a young woman and two young men watch with a camera and a notebook.

roots.context: We have tested what a night of sleep does to picture pairs, and met humans and other animals that sleep, even a jellyfish with no brain. Now we ask what sleep tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: At bedtime you learned eight picture pairs, then slept and knew nothing of the night. In the morning, most pairs were still there. You did not keep them on purpose, because you were asleep. So part of your mind keeps working while you are not aware of it.
deep_truth.habit: We think of 'me' as the part that is awake and noticing, and of sleep as a blank where nothing happens. But keeping what you learned went on all night, while you noticed nothing at all.
deep_truth.evidence: In the picture-pairs test, compare the pairs lost from the night set with the pairs lost from the day set. In studies of children aged 6 to 8, those who slept after learning kept more than those who stayed awake.

three.who_am_i: You are more than the part of you that is awake. Your mind keeps working through the night, even when you know nothing about it.
three.what_is_life: Every living being rests and works by turns. Crows, bats, bees, jellyfish and you all sleep and wake each day.
three.what_is_this_world: The world takes turns too: day and night, light and dark. Humans and other animals sleep and wake in time with it.

roots.thread: Sleep looks like stopping, but it is a different kind of working. In the picture-pairs test, your mind kept what you learned while you were not aware of anything. Upside-down jellyfish have no brain, yet they rest and wake on a daily rhythm and get sleepy when kept awake. Their bodies rest at night and are sleepy after a night kept awake. So the work of a mind is not only done by brains, and not only done while we are watching. Some scientists ask whether a rest without a brain should be called sleep.

teachings.teaching: Patanjali lists five kinds of activity of the mind: right knowing, mistaken knowing, imagining, sleep and memory. He says sleep is the activity of the mind that rests on the absence of other things.
teachings.link: Patanjali counts sleep as something the mind does, not as the mind being gone. The picture-pairs test shows the mind keeping memories during sleep.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that when a person is in deep sleep, they become one with pure being. They have gone back to their own self. That is why, the Upanishad says, we call it sleeping.
teachings.link: The Upanishad says a sleeper has 'gone to their own self'. In deep sleep you notice nothing, yet you are still there, and your body and mind keep working.

science.text: Sleep helps the brain keep what was learned in the day. Children who sleep after learning remember more than children who stay awake for the same hours.
Upside-down jellyfish, who have no brain, show a sleep-like state. Some scientists say true sleep should also show certain brain signals, so they argue about whether to call it sleep.

other_view.view: They say that what happens in sleep is the brain's chemistry and signals at work, with no one 'there'. Remembering in sleep is a process in nerve cells, and calling it the mind's work adds nothing to the explanation.

practice.title: Notice the edge of sleep
practice.say: Tonight, after lights off, lie on your back. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, five times. Feel your arms get heavy. Feel your legs get heavy. Notice your thoughts going slow and fuzzy. Try to notice the very moment you fall asleep. In the morning, tell me if you caught it.
practice.kid: Lie still after lights off. Breathe slowly five times. Feel your arms and legs get heavy. Can you catch the moment you fall asleep?

ask: Who kept the picture pairs safe while you were asleep?

A jellyfish with no brain still sleeps. What else might be doing a mind's work without a brain?
